c.tagline: Where the Red Sea meets the Horn of Africa's volcanic edge.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; agree the fare in Djiboutian francs with the driver before getting in. Shared taxis run fixed routes for a set per-seat price.

hood_desc: Beachfront district on the Heron peninsula with the city's top luxury resort, embassies and calm sea views; suits travelers wanting comfort, pools and easy airport transfers.
Hillside diplomatic quarter overlooking the Gulf of Tadjoura, home to upscale hotels and foreign missions; suits business travelers and those wanting a quiet, secure base near downtown.

The historic colonial-grid downtown around Place du 27 Juin (Place Ménélik) with markets, cafes, government buildings and budget-to-midrange hotels; suits budget travelers and those wanting to walk to sights and the port.
A quieter residential municipality along the coast south of the center with a handful of independent hotels; suits travelers wanting a calmer, more local base still near downtown.
The functional strip near Djibouti-Ambouli Airport with simple business and transit hotels; suits overnight layovers, early flights or military/NGO logistics stays.

water.note: Tap water is not safe to drink; use bottled or boiled water.

transit.pay: City buses and shared taxis are paid in cash (Djiboutian francs) directly to the driver or conductor; there is no rechargeable transit card. The Addis Ababa-Djibouti train is booked and paid for at Nagad station in advance.
transit.hours: City buses and shared taxis run roughly 6am-8pm; private taxis available later but should be pre-arranged through a hotel at night.
transit.note: Djibouti City has no metro or tram; most visitors rely on taxis. Nagad station, 10km south of downtown, serves the twice-weekly Addis Ababa passenger train.

landmarks: Hamoudi Mosque
The city's largest and most prominent mosque, completed in 1906 in Abbasid style by the merchant Haji Hamoudi, its twin minarets rising over the old town and the central market beside it.
Djibouti Central Market
The main produce and spice market in the old town, where stalls sell qat, fruit, woven straw mats and the curved Afar and Issa knives carried as ceremonial dress rather than souvenirs.
Place Menelik
The former heart of the French colonial quarter, laid out around 1900 with arcaded two-storey buildings designed to shade pedestrians, renamed Place du 27-Juin at independence.
Cathedral of Our Lady of the Good Shepherd
The seat of the Catholic diocese of Djibouti, built in 1964 to a modernist design by the French architect Joseph Müller on the site of the demolished Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc church.
People's Palace (Palais du Peuple)
A conference hall and monument built in 1984 as a gift from China to mark independence, its flag-lined plaza holding the Monument of the Martyrs to those who died resisting French rule.
Djibouti Museum
The national history and art museum on Rue de Moscou, holding archaeological finds and ethnographic collections tracing the region's prehistoric settlement and Afar and Somali cultural traditions.
Moucha Island
A coral island in the Gulf of Tadjoura about an hour by boat from the city, its fringing reef offering snorkelling and diving, with whale sharks passing between February and October.
Maskali Islands
A small coral archipelago half an hour by boat from the port, with shallow, calm reefs good for day-trip snorkelling among surgeonfish, parrotfish and sea turtles.
Lake Assal
A hypersaline crater lake 120 kilometres west of the city and the lowest point in Africa at 155 metres below sea level, its white salt flats and turquoise water ringed by black volcanic rock.
Arta Beach
A Gulf of Tadjoura beach about 90 minutes from the city near the town of Arta, known for the whale sharks that gather offshore between November and January.

intl.to: Dire Dawa & Addis Ababa (Ethiopia) - departs Nagad station, ~10 km south-west of the centre near the airport
intl.op: Ethio-Djibouti Standard Gauge Rail Transport S.C. — tickets at Nagad station

train.note: The Chinese-built standard-gauge Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway reopened to passengers in December 2016 and is the only train from Djibouti; it covers the 750 km to Addis Ababa in about 12 hours, against three days by road before it existed. Trains use Nagad station out near the airport rather than the old French colonial terminus in town, and they run only a few times a week, so check locally before planning around them. There is no online booking - tickets are sold at the station ticket office for cash, usually a day or two ahead, and passport and immigration formalities are handled at the station, so you need your Ethiopian visa arranged in advance. Djibouti has no domestic passenger rail: Nagad is the country's only passenger stop and the old metre-gauge CDE line is derelict.

intl.to: Dire Dawa & Addis Ababa (Ethiopia) - via the Galafi border
intl.op: Djiboutian and Ethiopian minibus and coach operators — tickets at the Djibouti City bus yard
shared 4x4s and minibuses — tickets at the Loyada road bus yard

bus.note: There is no formal coach station or online booking in Djibouti City; long-distance vehicles gather in the bus yards on the edge of the centre and leave when full, often before dawn to avoid the heat. Buses and minibuses cross into Ethiopia at Galafi on the main truck corridor, reaching Dire Dawa in around 10-12 hours and Addis Ababa in 14-18, a rough and dusty ride shared with the port's freight traffic. For Somaliland, shared vehicles run to the Loyada border, 20 km south-east, where you change to Somaliland transport for Borama and Hargeisa; a Somaliland visa is issued at the Hargeisa liaison office in Djibouti City, not at the border. Fares are cash in Djiboutian francs and there is no fixed timetable, so ask at your hotel the day before.

intl.to: Tadjoura (Djibouti) - departs L'Escale jetty in the old port, walking distance from the centre
intl.op: Djibouti ferry service — tickets at the jetty
Djibouti ferry service — tickets at the jetty

ferry.note: Small passenger ferries sail daily from L'Escale, the jetty in the old port a few minutes' walk from the city centre, across the Gulf of Tadjoura to Tadjoura and Obock, each taking around three hours and saving a very long drive around the gulf. Sailings are cash-only, sold at the jetty on the day, and can be cancelled in rough weather or high wind; boats are basic with open deck seating, so bring shade and water. Djibouti's main port and the Doraleh container terminal handle cargo only and are not open to passengers. Boats have historically crossed to Yemen, but these are irregular, unlicensed for tourists and unsafe given the conflict there.
